Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume full AC. Fix a finite cyclic subdivision of $S^1$ into edges. Let $c:S^1\times(0,1]\to S^2$ be continuous, with each $c_r$ an embedding. On every closed edge require that $c$ extends smoothly to an open neighborhood of that edge times each compact positive-radius interval, and has nonzero edge tangent there. At each subdivision vertex require the two one-sided tangent lines of $c_r$ to be distinct for every $r>0$; the family is smooth away from these finitely many corners. Then
$$D=\{0\}\cup\{r c_r(s):s\in S^1,\ 0<r\le1\}$$
forms a standard ball-disk pair: there is a homeomorphism $(B^3,D)\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\})$. In particular it is a properly embedded locally flat closed topological disk. There need be no positive lower bound on corner angles as $r\downarrow0$.

More precisely a radius-preserving homeomorphism of $B^3$ carries $D$ to a disk supplied by a smooth positive-radius family of embedded circles. If the subdivision has no corners and the family is already smooth, this preliminary homeomorphism may be the identity.

derivations.claim: At a seam choose its unit tangent and the ambient orientation. Project the inward transverse tangents of the two half-sheets to the normal plane and normalize to unit vectors $a(s),b(s)$, retaining the supplied labeling. They vary smoothly and are distinct. The normal field $e_x=(a-b)/|a-b|$ and its positive quarter-turn $e_y$ give a smooth normal frame along the entire seam, also around a circle. The two inward rays have respectively positive and negative $e_x$ component, since $a\cdot(a-b)=1-a\cdot b>0$ and $b\cdot(a-b)=a\cdot b-1<0$. Use a smooth ambient metric and its normal exponential map in this frame. By [F1] and compactness it gives one tubular coordinate system $(s,x,y)$ around the seam, with a short extension at arc ends. The projection of each half-sheet onto $(s,x)$ has invertible differential up to its boundary. Hence, after a uniform shrinking, their union is exactly a graph $y=f(s,x)$, smooth jointly in $s,x$ on each side of zero, continuous with $f(s,0)=0$, and with no other surface portions in the tube. The finite disjoint seam tubes can be made disjoint.

The nonsmooth locus is a compact subset of the seam interiors: the smooth locus is open in $S$, the seams are compact, and the arc ends and $K$ have protected smooth neighborhoods. Choose smaller seam tubes and a smooth cutoff $\mu(s)$ equal to one near every nonsmooth seam point and zero near the protected set and arc ends. Its transition regions along the seam are chosen where $S$ is already smooth. This is possible by finite interval charts and scalar bumps on the finitely many parameter circles or intervals. Shrink the tube widths so the support misses a neighborhood of $K$ and lies in the prescribed neighborhood; away from those parameter intervals no modification is required. There are finite uniform graph widths and slope bounds on the compact support. Choose a horizontal cutoff $\zeta(x)$ equal to one near zero and zero outside a narrower graph strip, and a small positive kernel width $\epsilon$. Let $f^\epsilon$ denote convolution in $x$ and set $g=f+\mu(s)\zeta(x)(f^\epsilon-f)$. By [F2], $f^\epsilon$ is jointly smooth across zero. Near a nonsmooth seam point both cutoffs equal one, so $g=f^\epsilon$. Where $\mu$ changes, $f$ is smooth in a neighborhood of that seam point; where $\zeta$ changes, $x\ne0$ and $f$ is smooth. It follows that $g$ is smooth everywhere on the modified graph. Take $\epsilon$ smaller if necessary so the graph error $\Delta=g-f$ has arbitrarily small uniform norm.

Choose a fixed vertical cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$. Take a small vertical width $a>0$, choose the horizontal strip so that $|f|<a/4$ there, and ensure $\|\chi'\|_\infty|\Delta|/a<1/2$. Define $T_t(s,x,y)=(s,x,y+t\chi((y-f(s,x))/a)\Delta(s,x))$, $0\le t\le1$, on the tube. Its derivative in $y$ is greater than $1/2$, so each vertical fiber map is an increasing homeomorphism equal to the identity near the fiber ends. The horizontal and parameter cutoffs make it the identity near the other tube boundaries as well. The fiber inverses are continuous jointly in $t,s,x,y$, by the same lower slope bound and monotonicity. Extend by the identity outside the tube. This is an ambient topological isotopy, and at $t=1$ it carries the graph of $f$ exactly to the graph of $g$. Its support can be made as small as specified by the choices in step 2.1. The formula requires no differentiability of $f$ at the seam.

Apply these constructions to the finitely many disjoint seam tubes. Their isotopies have disjoint support and therefore compose to one ambient isotopy, fixed on a neighborhood of $K$. At its endpoint each affected portion is the smooth graph $g$, agrees with the original smooth graph near all support boundaries, and introduces no intersection because it is the image under a homeomorphism. Outside the tubes the surface was smooth from the start. Thus the entire image is a smooth embedded surface, with the stated support and relative properties. Opposite inward rays cause no difficulty: their $e_x$ components still have opposite signs, and the same graph and convolution argument applies. Only coincident rays would invalidate the graph projection, and they were excluded explicitly.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 allows an empty seam list or empty nonsmooth locus, giving the identity isotopy.
Step 3.1 defines T_0 as the identity and retains positive fiber derivative for the whole time interval.
Step 4.1 includes one seam and finite disjoint compositions.
Step 4.1 explicitly allows opposite rays; Step 1.1 excludes only coincident rays and proves the projection signs.
Step 2.1 uses the actual smooth neighborhoods of arc ends to place the cutoff transition there, protecting the endpoints and K.
The Statement assumes full AC; Step 1.1 through Step 3.1 use only finite supplied seam charts and explicit scalar cutoffs and kernels.

axioms.use: Full AC is permitted and inherited from the recorded parametric corner-rounding supplier; the proof uses only finitely many supplied seam pieces, scalar cutoffs and convolutions. No arbitrary topological smoothing assertion is used.

risk_review.notes: Actual global seam graph coordinates use the two labeled half-sheets and distinct inward rays; the support transition occurs only where the old surface is already smooth. This is not a theorem about arbitrary locally flat TOP surfaces.
